units.en: Module upgrade costs usually are only available when upgrading a module to a differently-tiered one in the same category, e.g., upgrading an anti-air 1 module to anti-air 2, 3, or 4. They are usually less than new module costs, but in some cases like for light cruiser batteries, heavy cruiser batteries, and engines, they can be more expensive than a new module, sometimes doubly or triply so. Note: with engines, the upgrade costs only apply when staying within the same engine category. This is relevant for carrier conversions, as the more expensive upgrade costs are not paid when switching from cruiser or heavy ship engines to carrier engines, but they are paid if the design stays within the same engine category type and has a different tier.

⟦0⟧: with engines, the upgrade costs only apply when staying within the same engine category. This is relevant for carrier conversions, as the more expensive upgrade costs are not paid when switching from cruiser or heavy ship engines to carrier engines, but they are paid if the design stays within the same engine category type and has a different tier.
Production modifiers come from armor types and engines.

Dismantle costs are paid for removing specific modules, mainly armor modules and torpedo launchers (though the dismantle costs for torpedo launchers are fairly small). This includes removing battleship or battlecruiser armor when converting battleships or battlecruiser to carriers, which practically makes these carrier conversions more expensive than just producing a new carrier from scratch.

Equipment conversion speed bonuses from sources like ⟦0⟧, certain focuses like ⟦1⟧, etc. are applied as bonuses on the reduction of the ⟦2⟧ due to conversion. It only applies to equipment that can be converted, such as tanks with ⟦3⟧ and aircraft with ⟦4⟧, not ships, as alterations to ships are considered refits, not conversions. ⟦5⟧: the UI is currently bugged and does highlight conversion speed bonuses when refitting ships, even though their bonuses are not applied.

⟦0⟧ Consider upgrading an aircraft with a full cost of 30 . If, through conversion, the cost is normally reduced to 20 , the conversion savings amount to 10 , as ⟦1⟧. With one ⟦2⟧ conversion speed bonus, a reduction of 40% is applied to the 10 savings, giving a further 4 reduction. Therefore, if the initial conversion cost is 20 before researching the conversion bonus, it will be reduced to 16 after applying the bonus, as ⟦3⟧. With both conversion bonuses researched, it would be reduced to 12 , as ⟦4⟧.

With the right designs, these bonuses can help massively reduce the ⟦0⟧ cost of producing expensive equipment, like heavy tanks with heavy cannons or aircraft with self-sealing fuel tanks. Producing a barebones design first and then converting it into a full design can be just a few percentages more expensive than producing the full design outright, but have half or even less of the total resource cost. If a country has additional equipment conversion speed bonuses from elsewhere, making equipment in two steps can even be outright cheaper.

Ship refitting speed bonuses from sources like the ⟦0⟧ officer corps spirit, certain focuses like ⟦1⟧, etc., act as additional ⟦2⟧ bonuses that are only applied when refitting ships. This makes them have a smaller relative effect the more ⟦3⟧ the country already has.

With the right designs, these bonuses can help reduce the ⟦0⟧ costs of producing expensive ships like battleships or carriers, reduce the ⟦1⟧ of ships with final designs that are a lot more expensive than barebones ones as is often the case with carriers, or both.

Each nation can use a percentage of the resources on its territory for military production, with the rest being reserved exclusively for ⟦0⟧. This percentage depends on the ⟦1⟧, with ⟦2⟧ making all resources available for internal production and no resources available for ⟦3⟧.

The total amount of resources can be increased by researching the ⟦0⟧. Each level of excavation technology gives a resource gain efficiency increase of ⟦1⟧ to the total of all extracted resources (extracted resources are those that come from the ground via drilling or mining; it does not include resources from ⟦2⟧ or ⟦3⟧). There are five (5) levels of excavation technology; researching all of them will give a ⟦4⟧ bonus to the extracted resources total.

The total amount of resources can also be increased by building ⟦0⟧. Each level of infrastructure gives a resource increase of ⟦1⟧ to the total of all extracted resources (except those resources produced by a synthetic refinery or resources acquired via trade) in a state. There are five (5) levels of infrastructure; building all of them will give a ⟦2⟧ bonus to the extracted resources total. Additionally, a ⟦3⟧ can be constructed at state level, increasing the resources gained per infrastructure by ⟦4⟧.
A ⟦0⟧ modifier is applied to resource extraction in a state if there is a ⟦1⟧ or ⟦2⟧ in it connected to the capital via sea or railroad. Most states have this bonus at game start.
Resources cannot be stockpiled. They flow directly to production, with any excess resources being effectively wasted. ⟦0⟧ that is produced directly from ⟦1⟧ can be stockpiled, however.

Different kinds of equipment require different resources to produce. Lacking sufficient resources will apply an increasing efficiency penalty up to ⟦0⟧ to the lowest priority production lines. The penalty increases by ⟦1⟧ per missing unit of resource per type, and the highest applicable penalty is applied to individual factories.

For example, when having 2 units of ⟦0⟧ and 0 units of ⟦1⟧ available and adding a new production line for Support Equipment (needs 2 1 ) with 11 ⟦2⟧, the first factory receives a penalty of ⟦3⟧ because it misses one unit of ⟦4⟧. The second factory receives a ⟦5⟧ penalty because it is missing both two units of ⟦6⟧ and the one unit of ⟦7⟧. For each of the remaining factories, the penalty increases by ⟦8⟧ because they need two additional ⟦9⟧, the last ones getting a ⟦10⟧ penalty, being unable to produce the equipment at all. The production line shows the average penalty across all factories, ⟦11⟧. This penalty stacks multiplicatively with other modifiers.
Some countries have access to unique ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ and/or ⟦2⟧ that can reduce these penalties.

When facing a shortage, consider that the cost in ⟦0⟧, hence construction slowdown, to provide sufficient resources might not be worth the benefit of eliminating the penalty inflicted on the production line. Note that production efficiency increase is not affected by availability of resources for a production line, so it can make sense to leave a production line without adequate resources when it is first started and put the civilian factories needed to buy resources to another use, as this is when output loss is lowest. However, consider that countries from which you buy resources gain the construction you spend. Hence, buying resources from a country that's in the same faction, or which will be so later, doesn't result in loss from your faction, though both AI and humans, even allied, may have different ideas about how to put those civilian factories to use.

When powered: Civilian factories have have their base output of 4[29] increased to 5[30]. Military factories have have their base output of 3.5[31] increased to 4.5[32]. Naval dockyards have have their base output of 2[33] increased to 2.5[34].

There are several ways to acquire more resources:
Build a ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ in a resource-producing state that has none, and connect it to the capital.
Change ⟦0⟧ to keep more domestic production.
Gain rights to resources through ⟦0⟧ or unique ⟦1⟧.
In addition to acquiring more resources when there is a shortage, there are many ways to reduce how many are consumed by a nation's production lines:
Lower-tier equipment, components, and chassis often have reduced resource costs.
Aircraft designs with Non-Strategic Material Usage have reduced ⟦0⟧ costs.
Omitting resource-costing components from ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and ⟦2⟧ designs like ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, or ⟦5⟧ reduces their resource costs.

Because converting equipment only costs resources if the new design has a different resource cost from the old one, producing tanks and/or aircraft in multiple steps, where a bare-bones design is built first before it is converted to the full design, can reduce overall resource costs for that line of equipment.

Refitting ships after they have been produced only consumes the resources of the refitted components. For example, building a cruiser with no armor and the refitting it with ⟦0⟧ only incurs the armor's ⟦1⟧ cost during the refit step, whereas building the same ship without refitting would cost additional ⟦2⟧ during the entire production process instead of just when the armor is being added.

Some ⟦0⟧ (MIO) bonuses can reduce resource requirements for certain types of equipment. The Vertical Integration and Permanent Industrial Revolution MIO policies also reduce resource requirements for all MIO equipment, though Vertical Integration also increases the production penalty for lacking resources.

Land divisions and air wings are not produced as atomic units. Instead, factories produce individual tanks, airplanes, and so forth. This equipment is then sent to fill out the country's land divisions and air wings. Unlike resources, equipment can be stockpiled. The stockpiles can be viewed under the Logistics Tab .
